description:
We’re Sanchit, Mihir, Vittal, Prayag, and Ram from Denmark High School doing MODIS-VIIRS Harmonization. We love Earth science, data and coding. 

NASA’s aging fire satellites drifted off schedule, so their records don't match, and we’ve found evidence of fake fire trends in real data. Join us to build the fix.

Our skills: Python, data analysis, statistics, satellite data.

Seeking one web developer skilled in JavaScript, maps, and charts, who also enjoys design or presenting.
summary:
For 25 years, NASA satellites have counted almost every fire on Earth. That record is how scientists answer a simple question: are fires getting worse? But it has a problem. The two satellites that started the record, Terra and Aqua, are running low on fuel, so their orbits are drifting and they now scan about an hour earlier or later than they’re supposed to. Most fires flare up in the afternoon, so a satellite arriving at a different time counts a different number, even if nothing on the ground changed. NASA also added a sharper instrument in 2012 (VIIRS) that spots several times more fires than Terra and Aqua’s MODIS, creating a fake “jump” in the record.

We built SUNDIAL, an app and data pipeline that fixes both problems. It converts the older satellites’ counts into the new instrument’s units. Then, using only the satellites’ own data, it measures how far each one’s timing has drifted and how fast fire counts change per hour, and rebuilds one consistent monthly fire record for 182 countries. In an independent test against the newer satellite, it shrank the fake trend in 102 of 167 countries, which hold 85% of the world’s fires, and closed two-thirds of the gap in Australia. It also flags where it can’t be trusted yet, like India, where farmers have started burning later in the day.

Fire records shape wildfire planning and climate research. If a satellite’s clock is off, those decisions rest on numbers that aren’t real. SUNDIAL shows how fire is actually changing.
details:
NASA has been counting fires from space since 2000. Each time a satellite passes over, it flags the hot spots it sees. Scientists add up those scan records to see whether fires are getting worse. SUNDIAL makes that record consistent from start to finish.

Two things break the raw record. The first is a change of camera. MODIS has flown since 2000. VIIRS joined in 2012 with much sharper pixels and sees several times more fires, so if you combine both records together, fires seem to jump in 2012. The second is drift. To save fuel, the two satellites carrying MODIS stopped correcting their orbits in 2020 and 2021. The Terra satellite now passes earlier in the morning and the Aqua satellite passes later in the afternoon. Most fires peak in the afternoon, so Terra sees fewer fires and Aqua sees more. Both changes look like real trends, but they aren’t.

We fix the camera change by measuring how MODIS compares with VIIRS from 2012 to 2019, when both were on time and neither had drifted. We do this for every country, season, and day or night, and use it to convert MODIS fire counts into “VIIRS units.” For 2000 to 2011, an AI model fine-tunes that conversion month by month. Tested on years it never saw, its monthly estimates came within about 17% of what VIIRS actually counted, and its yearly totals within about 9%.

The drift fix uses the satellites’ own images. A MODIS image is about 2,330 km wide, so the east side of a pass is seen later in local time than the west side. We compare fire counts on the two sides, using pixels of the same width so pixel size cancels out. That tells us how fast fires build up through the day. Fires peak around 3 pm, so we use a curve to estimate how many more fires are burning at one hour than another. Terra now passes up to an hour earlier than its scheduled 10:30, so it catches fewer fires. For each month, we use the curve to estimate how many fires it would have seen at 10:30, and scale its count up to match.

The result is a monthly fire record for 182 countries from 2000 to 2025, with an error range on every value. Tested against VIIRS, which never drifted, the fix shrinks Terra’s false trend in 114 of the 150 countries we could test. The web app lets you pick any country, see the raw and corrected records side by side, and see how far to trust each one.

Benefits

The record runs 25 years instead of the 14 you get from VIIRS alone. Long-term trends need long, consistent records, and SUNDIAL provides one. Some countries have millions of fires to calibrate with, others only a handful. So each country gets a label: ‘measured’ if it has enough fires to work out its own correction, ‘blended’ if it has some, and ‘borrowed’ if it has so few that it relies mostly on the average of all countries. The label shows up on the site, so users know how much to trust each country’s trend. An anomaly score flags months with unusually many or few fires compared with the same month in other years. Everything is built from open NASA fire data and Natural Earth borders, so anyone can rebuild it without an account.

Intended impact

We want anyone looking at a 25-year fire chart to trust that the changes on it are real. Since 2020, part of every MODIS fire trend is just the satellites drifting. Researchers studying climate and fire, and agencies planning for fire seasons, could mistake that drift for a real decline. We didn’t find a drift correction applied to country fire counts, so SUNDIAL fills that gap.

SUNDIAL is also honest about where the satellites themselves fall short. In Punjab, India, farmers now burn crop stubble in the late afternoon, after every satellite has already passed. So the record undercounts one of the main causes of north India’s winter smog. Instead of hiding that, the site points it out.

Tools and technology

  • Pipeline: Python (Polars, DuckDB, NumPy) in five steps: download, clean, boundaries, calibrate and build.
  • Conversion model: scikit-learn.
  • API: FastAPI and Uvicorn.
  • Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with D3, hosted on Vercel and GitHub Pages.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m), NOAA’s GOES-16 fire product through AWS, and Natural Earth borders.
  • Version control: git and GitHub, which we also used to timestamp our test rules before we touched the data.

What makes it creative

The satellites carry their own clock. Each MODIS image is so wide that its east edge is seen about 40 minutes later in the day than its west edge. By comparing fire counts on the two edges, we measured how fast fires grow through the day without any outside data. The sun lights the two edges differently, which could skew that measurement. But Terra and Aqua fly in opposite directions, so the error flips sign between them, and combining the two cancels it out.

We also treated our work like a lab experiment. Before downloading a single fire in Australia, we wrote our pass and fail rules into a locked file we called “the vault”, then ran the test exactly once. Our drift fix closed two-thirds of the fake drop. An earlier version of the method failed the same test, so we dropped it.

Factors we considered

Honesty came first. With 182 countries, it’s easy to land on a version of the method that only looks good by luck. So we wrote down our pass and fail rules before seeing any results, and tested only on years and places the method had never seen. We also ran it on years with no drift, to make sure it didn’t invent changes there. We report every failure, including experiments that missed their own rules.

Small countries have too few fires to measure well, so instead of dropping them, we blend their numbers with the average of all countries, leaning on the average more when a country has less data. We also accepted that people change their habits. The method assumes burning times stay the same, and in places like Punjab, they don’t.
